title: Social Security Legislation Amendment (Strengthening the Job Seeker Compliance Framework) Bill 2014
short_title: Social Security Legislation Amendment (Strengthening the Job Seeker Compliance Framework) Bill 2014

divisions.question: Eric Abetz I move: That this bill be now read a third time. Christopher Back The question is that the bill be read a third time.

speeches.speaker: Luke Hartsuyker
speeches.brief: Moved a bill toughening job seeker compliance, noting 4.47 million of 12.75 million scheduled employment provider appointments were missed in 2013-14, a 35 per cent non-attendance rate, and that almost 280,000 job seekers, more than one in five, had a participation failure applied that year, while promoting the Restart program's incentive of up to $10,000 for employers hiring mature-age workers.

speeches.speaker: Julie Collins
speeches.brief: Argued that Labor supports mutual obligation and the bill's no-show, no-pay principle but opposes removing review rights, weakening protections for older job seekers, and extending delegation powers, while seeking assurances that suspensions will be notified promptly.

speeches.speaker: Karen McNamara
speeches.brief: Supported stronger compliance for missed employment appointments, including suspension until attendance and removal of back pay for non-compliance, while arguing that reasonable excuses and safeguards for vulnerable job seekers would remain protected.

speeches.speaker: Joanne Ryan
speeches.brief: Questioned how job seekers delayed by severe weather, transport problems or other circumstances could give prior notice, and warned that suspending payments without adequate notice could further disadvantage people facing hardship.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill as punitive, arguing that it would penalise vulnerable job seekers, remove review rights and outsource compliance decisions to employment providers, while calling for job creation and describing barriers faced by job seekers in Bendigo.

speeches.speaker: Alex Hawke
speeches.brief: Supported the bill as a measure to reinforce mutual obligation, arguing that people who miss appointments without satisfactory reasons should be required to comply, while saying that those facing serious disadvantage were not the intended target.

speeches.speaker: Angus Taylor
speeches.brief: Supported the Job Seeker Compliance Framework bill, citing that almost 4.5 million of 12 million compulsory appointments in 2013-14 were missed, a 35 per cent non-attendance rate, cited British economist Stephen Nickell's research linking strict benefit enforcement to lower unemployment, and said from 1 January 2015 job seekers without a reasonable excuse would lose back-payment for missed appointments.

speeches.speaker: Tony Pasin
speeches.brief: Supported the Job Seeker Compliance Framework bill, citing that 4.47 million of 12,750,000 compulsory appointments went unattended in 2013-14, a 35 per cent non-attendance rate, and that almost 280,000 job seekers, more than one in five, had a participation failure applied that year, and said from 1 January 2015 suspended payments would only be reinstated once a missed appointment was rescheduled and attended.

speeches.speaker: Eric Hutchinson
speeches.brief: Supported the Job Seeker Compliance Framework bill's two-stage rollout, from 1 January 2015 requiring an attended appointment before reinstating suspended payments and from 1 July 2015 withholding back pay for unexcused absences, citing an attendance rate of only 65 per cent at compulsory appointments last financial year, and highlighted Trade Support Loans of up to $20,000 for apprentices.

speeches.speaker: Laurie Ferguson
speeches.brief: Presented the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights' examination of the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment (Foreign Fighters) Bill 2014, concluding that its declared area offence, carrying up to 10 years imprisonment, is likely incompatible with human rights because it reverses the presumption of innocence, and raised concerns about a new advocating terrorism offence that could criminalise speech through a recklessness test.
